- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially in the first 5–10 days, then underestimates later.
- Forecasts tend to overshoot after sharp price spikes (e.g., 85+), then sharply correct downward — model fails to capture this “rebound” or “mean reversion” effect.
- Model underestimates true mean price levels, particularly in the 70–75 range, suggesting it’s too optimistic about downward trends.
- Forecast bias is often toward higher prices than true outcome, especially when historical mean is above 75.
- Model exhibits lag in responding to recent price drops — it takes 2–3 days to adjust downward after a sharp decline.
- Forecasts show persistent “overfitting” to recent high prices, failing to account for seasonal or policy-driven mean reversion.
- When true outcome is below 70, model often fails to recognize the trend and continues to forecast above 75.
- Model tends to underestimate the magnitude of price corrections after spikes — e.g., after 85, it often forecasts 75–80 instead of 70–72.
- Forecasts are overly smooth — fail to capture volatility spikes or sudden drops, especially in the 3rd–5th day of the horizon.
- Model exhibits “false optimism” in the final 5–7 days — forecasts often rise above true outcome, even when historical trend is downward.
